Week 2 - In Class Activity: End-to-end Machine Learning Pipeline in R

Abigail Kreuser

Goal: Create an end-to-end machine learning regression pipeline in R using tidymodels.

In this activity, you will use an abalone dataset. The age of abalone is usually determined by cutting the shell through the cone, staining it, and counting the number of rings under a microscope. We will use easier-to-measure variables to predict the number of rings.

By the end of the activity, you should be able to:

  1. Load and explore a dataset in R.
  2. Separate predictors from the response variable.
  3. Create new features from existing variables.
  4. Build a reusable preprocessing recipe.
  5. Fit and tune a machine learning model using cross-validation.
  6. Evaluate model performance on held-out test data.
  7. Interpret model behavior using predictions, residuals, and variable importance.
  8. Modify the pipeline to use a different model.

R machine learning library: This R Markdown document uses tidymodels, the most common modern R ecosystem for machine learning workflows.

Dataset: Warwick J Nash, Tracy L Sellers, Simon R Talbot, Andrew J Cawthorn and Wes B Ford (1994) “The Population Biology of Abalone (Haliotis species) in Tasmania. I. Blacklip Abalone (H. rubra) from the North Coast and Islands of Bass Strait”, Sea Fisheries Division, Technical Report No. 48 (ISSN 1034-3288).

The dataset does not include column names in the raw CSV, so we add them manually while reading the file.

  "shucked_weight", "viscera_weight", "shell_weight", "rings"
)

abalone <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dblaskey/ML_Course_Code/main/Data/abalone.csv",

4. Model Preprocessing and Regression

We now build a model for the number of abalone rings.

The response variable is rings.

The predictors are:

Name Data Type Units Description
sex nominal M, F, and I infant
length continuous mm Longest shell measurement
diameter continuous mm Perpendicular to length
height continuous mm With meat in shell
whole_weight continuous grams Whole abalone
shucked_weight continuous grams Weight of meat
viscera_weight continuous grams Gut weight after bleeding
shell_weight continuous grams After being dried

Train/Test Split

We split the data into training and testing sets. Because rings is numeric, we use strata = rings so the split tries to keep similar distributions of abalone ages in both sets.

set.seed(42)

abalone_split <- initial_split(
  abalone,
  prop = 0.80,
  strata = rings
)

abalone_train <- training(abalone_split)
abalone_test  <- testing(abalone_split)

abalone_train

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering creates new predictors from existing predictors. We will talk more about this next week.

In tidymodels, feature engineering usually belongs inside a recipe. This is important because the same transformations are applied consistently during training, cross-validation, and prediction.

abalone_recipe <- recipe(rings ~ ., data = abalone_train) |>
  # Shape proxy
  step_mutate(volume_proxy = length * diameter * height) |>
  # Composition ratios. The small constant prevents division by zero.
  step_mutate(shell_to_whole = shell_weight / (whole_weight + 1e-6)) |>
  step_mutate(weight_per_size = whole_weight / (volume_proxy + 1e-6)) |>
  # Residual-weight feature
  step_mutate(nonmeat_weight = whole_weight - shucked_weight - viscera_weight) |>
  # Preprocessing
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = FALSE) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

abalone_recipe
## 
## ── Recipe ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 
## ── Inputs
## Number of variables by role
## outcome:   1
## predictor: 8
## 
## ── Operations
## • Variable mutation for: length * diameter * height
## • Variable mutation for: shell_weight / (whole_weight + 1e-06)
## • Variable mutation for: whole_weight / (volume_proxy + 1e-06)
## • Variable mutation for: whole_weight - shucked_weight - viscera_weight
## • Median imputation for: all_numeric_predictors()
## • Mode imputation for: all_nominal_predictors()
## • Dummy variables from: all_nominal_predictors()
## • Centering and scaling for: all_numeric_predictors()

Build the Random Forest Workflow

We are using a random forest model, but do not worry too much about the details of this model or its hyperparameters yet. We will discuss random forests later in the semester. Right now, we are using it to demonstrate the end-to-end machine learning pipeline.

The workflow combines:

  1. A preprocessing recipe.
  2. A model specification.
  3. A tuning grid.
  4. Cross-validation.
rf_model <- rand_forest(
  trees = tune(),
  mtry = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") |>
  set_mode("regression")

rf_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(abalone_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_model)

rf_workflow
## ══ Workflow ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## Preprocessor: Recipe
## Model: rand_forest()
## 
## ── Preprocessor ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 8 Recipe Steps
## 
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_impute_median()
## • step_impute_mode()
## • step_dummy()
## • step_normalize()
## 
## ── Model ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Random Forest Model Specification (regression)
## 
## Main Arguments:
##   mtry = tune()
##   trees = tune()
##   min_n = tune()
## 
## Engine-Specific Arguments:
##   importance = permutation
## 
## Computational engine: ranger

Cross-Validation

Cross-validation gives a more realistic estimate of predictive performance than judging the model only on the training data. The training dataset is split into five folds. The model is trained on four folds and validated on the remaining fold, repeated five times.

In this example, we tune the random forest using RMSE. Lower RMSE means better predictive performance.

set.seed(42)

abalone_folds <- vfold_cv(
  abalone_train,
  v = 5,
  strata = rings
)

rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  trees(range = c(300, 500)),
  mtry(range = c(2, 6)),
  min_n(range = c(4, 8)),
  levels = c(trees = 2, mtry = 3, min_n = 3)
)

rf_grid
## # A tibble: 18 × 3
##    trees  mtry min_n
##    <int> <int> <int>
##  1   300     2     4
##  2   500     2     4
##  3   300     4     4
##  4   500     4     4
##  5   300     6     4
##  6   500     6     4
##  7   300     2     6
##  8   500     2     6
##  9   300     4     6
## 10   500     4     6
## 11   300     6     6
## 12   500     6     6
## 13   300     2     8
## 14   500     2     8
## 15   300     4     8
## 16   500     4     8
## 17   300     6     8
## 18   500     6     8
# WARNING: This cell may take a few minutes to run.

set.seed(42)

rf_tuned <- tune_grid(
  rf_workflow,
  resamples = abalone_folds,
  grid = rf_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)

collect_metrics(rf_tuned) |>
  arrange(mean)
## # A tibble: 54 × 9
##     mtry trees min_n .metric .estimator  mean     n std_err .config         
##    <int> <int> <int> <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>           
##  1     6   300     4 rsq     standard   0.558     5  0.0172 pre0_mod13_post0
##  2     6   300     6 rsq     standard   0.558     5  0.0162 pre0_mod14_post0
##  3     2   500     4 rsq     standard   0.559     5  0.0164 pre0_mod04_post0
##  4     4   300     4 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0170 pre0_mod07_post0
##  5     2   300     4 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0168 pre0_mod01_post0
##  6     6   300     8 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0171 pre0_mod15_post0
##  7     6   500     6 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0167 pre0_mod17_post0
##  8     6   500     4 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0167 pre0_mod16_post0
##  9     6   500     8 rsq     standard   0.560     5  0.0169 pre0_mod18_post0
## 10     2   300     8 rsq     standard   0.561     5  0.0172 pre0_mod03_post0
## # ℹ 44 more rows
best_rf <- select_best(rf_tuned, metric = "rmse")
best_rf #   4   300     6 pre0_mod08_post0
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##    mtry trees min_n .config         
##   <int> <int> <int> <chr>           
## 1     4   300     6 pre0_mod08_post0
final_rf_workflow <- finalize_workflow(rf_workflow, best_rf)

final_rf_fit <- last_fit(
  final_rf_workflow,
  split = abalone_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)
)

collect_metrics(final_rf_fit)
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   .metric .estimator .estimate .config        
##   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl> <chr>          
## 1 rmse    standard       2.16  pre0_mod0_post0
## 2 mae     standard       1.50  pre0_mod0_post0
## 3 rsq     standard       0.578 pre0_mod0_post0

Evaluate Predictions

Now we collect predictions for the held-out test set and visualize how close the model predictions were to the observed number of rings.

rf_predictions <- collect_predictions(final_rf_fit) |>
  mutate(residual = rings - .pred)

rf_predictions |>
  select(rings, .pred, residual) |>
  head()
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##   rings .pred residual
##   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1    15  9.20    5.80 
## 2     9 10.8    -1.83 
## 3    19 14.3     4.73 
## 4    14 11.4     2.55 
## 5     7  8.95   -1.95 
## 6    10  9.17    0.826
rf_metrics <- collect_metrics(final_rf_fit)

rmse_value <- rf_metrics |> filter(.metric == "rmse") |> pull(.estimate)
mae_value  <- rf_metrics |> filter(.metric == "mae")  |> pull(.estimate)
rsq_value  <- rf_metrics |> filter(.metric == "rsq")  |> pull(.estimate)

ggplot(rf_predictions, aes(x = rings, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = min(rf_predictions$rings),
    y = max(rf_predictions$.pred),
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    label = paste0(
      "MAE = ", round(mae_value, 2),
      "\nRMSE = ", round(rmse_value, 2),
      "\nR-squared = ", round(rsq_value, 2)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Actual Rings",
    y = "Predicted Rings",
    title = "Predicted vs. Actual Rings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(rf_predictions, aes(x = rings, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Actual Rings",
    y = "Residual (actual - predicted)",
    title = "Residuals: Positive Values Indicate Underprediction"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Variable Importance

Variable importance indicates which predictors provided the model with useful information during training. We will discuss this in more detail later in the semester.

final_rf_model <- extract_workflow(final_rf_fit) |>
  extract_fit_parsnip()

importance <- final_rf_model$fit$variable.importance |>
  enframe(name = "feature", value = "importance") |>
  arrange(desc(importance)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(feature = reorder(feature, importance))

ggplot(importance, aes(x = feature, y = importance)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Feature",
    y = "Permutation importance",
    title = "Random Forest Variable Importance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

5. Reflection Questions

Answer these in a few sentences each.

  1. What are the required steps in this machine learning pipeline? Split the data by stratified groups of the numeric response variable (abalone rings) to keep the testing and trainging groups similar distributions. Engineer features to make new predictor variables with imputationof a median, mode, and dummy variable then all are normalized which I assume fit better in the recipe. Then build the model workflow by incorporating a preprocessing recipe, model specifications, a tuning grid, and cross validation.

  2. What train/test split was used for this model? An 80/20 percent split stratified following the distribution of ring data.

  3. What does cross-validation do, and why do we use it? It seperates the training data further, reserving a fold for testing folds of training data which gives a better understanding of model performance than just one validation of testing/training data.

  4. Which metric did we use to choose the best model? RMSE: root mean squared error

  5. Did the model perform well? What evidence supports your answer? Using RMSE, I would say yes, because it is on the same scale as the target variable and 2 rings off doesn’t seem too bad if I am only considering the numbers. However, for harvesting and management, I would need to know more to understand the reproductive value with age of abalone, and determine if being off two years in age estimation at certain ages would have population implications.

  6. Look at the residual plot. Does the model make larger errors for younger or older abalone? The model makes larger errors for older abalone with large ranges after about 12 rings.

  7. Which predictors appear most important? Do those results make sense biologically? All of the weight variables appear the most important, non-meat weight having the most importance which was calculated by subtracting the shucked weight and viscera (gut weight after bleeding) from the whole weight. I think the results somewhat make sense biologically, but I don’t understand why non-meat weight would be much more important than the dry shell weight. With the subtraction of the shucked weight adn viscera, the non-meat weight would be shell weight and anything wet that remained in the abalone after shucking, plus blood from the gut. Shell weight makes sense as being influential because the rings are made as the shell grows, however I would think the viscera would be accounted for in shucked weight and the weight of blood would be related to viscera size and meat.

  add_recipe(abalone_recipe) |>
  add_model(knn_model)

knn_workflow
## ══ Workflow ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
## Preprocessor: Recipe
## Model: nearest_neighbor()
## 
## ── Preprocessor ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## 8 Recipe Steps
## 
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_mutate()
## • step_impute_median()
## • step_impute_mode()
## • step_dummy()
## • step_normalize()
## 
## ── Model ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## K-Nearest Neighbor Model Specification (regression)
## 
## Main Arguments:
##   neighbors = tune()
##   weight_func = tune()
##   dist_power = tune()
## 
## Computational engine: kknn 
## 
## Model fit template:
## kknn::train.kknn(formula = missing_arg(), data = missing_arg(), 
##     ks = min_rows(tune(), data, 5), kernel = tune(), distance = tune())
# TODO: Create a tuning grid for KNN.
set.seed(42)

abalone_folds <- vfold_cv(
  abalone_train,
  v = 5,
  strata = rings
)

knn_grid <- grid_regular(
  neighbors(range = c(1, 50)),
  weight_func(values = c("rectangular", "triangular", "epanechnikov", "gaussian")),
  dist_power(range = c(1, 2)),
  levels = c(neighbors = 10, weight_func = 4, dist_power = 2)
)

knn_grid
## # A tibble: 80 × 3
##    neighbors weight_func dist_power
##        <int> <chr>            <dbl>
##  1         1 rectangular          1
##  2         6 rectangular          1
##  3        11 rectangular          1
##  4        17 rectangular          1
##  5        22 rectangular          1
##  6        28 rectangular          1
##  7        33 rectangular          1
##  8        39 rectangular          1
##  9        44 rectangular          1
## 10        50 rectangular          1
## # ℹ 70 more rows
# KNN model specification
knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(
  neighbors   = tune(),
  weight_func = tune(),
  dist_power  = tune()
) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%   # use "regression" for numeric outcomes
  set_engine("kknn")



# Tune across the grid using cross-validation

# TODO: Tune the KNN model with cross-validation.
knn_tuned <- tune_grid(
  knn_workflow,
  resamples = abalone_folds,
  grid = knn_grid,
    metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
  #metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc)  # choose metrics for your outcome
)

collect_metrics(knn_tuned) |>
  arrange(mean)

# TODO: Select the best KNN model, fit it to the training set, and evaluate it on the test set.
best_knn <- select_best(knn_tuned, metric = "rmse")
best_knn #1        39 triangular           1 pre0_mod63_post0
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   neighbors weight_func dist_power .config         
##       <int> <chr>            <dbl> <chr>           
## 1        39 triangular           1 pre0_mod63_post0
final_knn_workflow <- finalize_workflow(knn_workflow, best_knn)

final_knn_fit <- last_fit(
  final_knn_workflow ,
  split = abalone_split,
  metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)
)
collect_metrics(final_knn_fit)
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##   .metric .estimator .estimate .config        
##   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl> <chr>          
## 1 rmse    standard       2.23  pre0_mod0_post0
## 2 mae     standard       1.49  pre0_mod0_post0
## 3 rsq     standard       0.569 pre0_mod0_post0
final_knn_model <- extract_workflow(final_knn_fit) |>
  extract_fit_parsnip()

knn_predictions <- collect_predictions(final_knn_fit) |>
  mutate(residual = rings - .pred)

knn_predictions |>
  select(rings, .pred, residual) |>
  head()
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##   rings .pred residual
##   <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1    15  8.37    6.63 
## 2     9 11.2    -2.23 
## 3    19 11.8     7.18 
## 4    14 12.1     1.85 
## 5     7  7.49   -0.492
## 6    10  9.37    0.630
knn_metrics <- collect_metrics(final_knn_fit)

rmse_value <- knn_metrics |> filter(.metric == "rmse") |> pull(.estimate)
mae_value  <- knn_metrics |> filter(.metric == "mae")  |> pull(.estimate)
rsq_value  <- knn_metrics |> filter(.metric == "rsq")  |> pull(.estimate)

# super simmilar output... 

ggplot(knn_predictions, aes(x = rings, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = min(knn_predictions$rings),
    y = max(knn_predictions$.pred),
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    label = paste0(
      "MAE = ", round(mae_value, 2),
      "\nRMSE = ", round(rmse_value, 2),
      "\nR-squared = ", round(rsq_value, 2)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Actual Rings",
    y = "Predicted Rings",
    title = "Predicted vs. Actual Rings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
